summary: Defines CHAP, a way for one side of a PPP link to check the identity of the other. The checker sends a random challenge, and the peer replies with a hash computed from the challenge and a shared secret, so the secret itself is never sent.

eli5.summary: A guard gives you a random number, and you must answer with a result only someone who knows the secret code can work out. You prove you know the secret without ever saying it.

questions: what is the chap packet format
subtitle: How one end of a PPP link checks the other's identity with a random challenge and a hashed reply.

tldr.problem: A PPP link may need to verify who is on the other end before network traffic flows, without sending the secret across the link.
tldr.mechanism: The authenticator sends a random challenge. The peer replies with a one-way hash over the identifier, the shared secret and the challenge, and the authenticator compares it with its own calculation. It can repeat this at random intervals.
tldr.outcome: The secret never crosses the link and repeated challenges limit exposure, but both ends must hold the secret in plaintext form. It obsoletes RFC 1334 and is updated by RFC 2484.

today: RFC 1994 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1334 and is updated by RFC 2484.

sections.title: Authentication on a PPP Link
sections.content:
After the Link Establishment phase, PPP provides an optional Authentication phase before the Network-Layer Protocol phase. Authentication is not mandatory by default. To require it, an implementation MUST specify the Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option during Link Establishment.

These protocols are intended mainly for hosts and routers that connect to a PPP network server over switched circuits or dial-up lines, though they could be used on dedicated links. The RFC calls the end that requires authentication the authenticator and the other end the peer.
sections.eli5: Before letting you into the club, the doorkeeper may ask who you are. Asking is optional, but if the club wants it, it must say so at the door.

sections.title: The Three-Way Handshake
sections.content:
CHAP verifies the peer's identity with a 3-way handshake, done on initial link establishment and repeatable at any time afterwards:

  1. The authenticator sends a challenge.
  2. The peer answers with a value calculated with a one-way hash function.
  3. The authenticator compares it with its own calculation. If they match it acknowledges the authentication, otherwise the connection SHOULD be terminated.
  4. At random intervals the authenticator sends a new challenge and repeats the steps.

The response is the one-way hash over the Identifier, followed by the secret, followed by the Challenge Value. For MD5 it is 16 octets long. The secret is known only to the two ends and is not sent over the link.
sections.eli5: The guard says a random number. You mix it with your secret in a way that cannot be undone and say the result. The guard does the same mixing and checks that the answers match.

sections.title: Strengths, Weaknesses and Design Rules
sections.content:
CHAP protects against playback by the peer through an incrementally changing identifier and a variable challenge value, and repeated challenges limit the time of exposure to any single attack. Negotiating CHAP in both directions gives mutual authentication with the same secrets, and name fields can index a large table of secrets.

The drawbacks are that the secret must be available in plaintext form, so irreversibly encrypted password databases cannot be used, and that it suits large installations poorly because every secret is kept at both ends.

The secret MUST be at least 1 octet and SHOULD be as large and unguessable as a well-chosen password. It is preferred to be at least the hash length, 16 octets for MD5. Each challenge SHOULD be unique, with global and temporal uniqueness, and SHOULD be unpredictable.
sections.eli5: The trick works well because the secret is never spoken and the question keeps changing. The downside is that both sides must keep the actual secret written down somewhere.

sections.title: Option and Packet Formats
sections.content:
CHAP is negotiated with an Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option of Type 3, Length 5, protocol c223 (hex) and a one-octet Algorithm field. The one value required to be implemented is 5, CHAP with MD5.

Each CHAP packet travels in a PPP frame with protocol type c223 and has a one-octet Code, a one-octet Identifier, a two-octet Length and a Data field. Codes are 1 Challenge, 2 Response, 3 Success and 4 Failure. Challenge and Response data hold a Value-Size octet, the Value and a Name. Success and Failure data hold a human readable Message that MUST NOT affect protocol operation.
sections.eli5: Every message has a label saying what kind it is, a number to match questions with answers, and its length.

sections.title: Challenge, Response, Success and Failure
sections.content:
The authenticator MUST send Challenge packets until a valid Response arrives or an optional retry counter expires, and may send one at any time in the Network-Layer Protocol phase. The Identifier and Challenge Value MUST change each time a Challenge is sent. The Response copies the Identifier of the Challenge it answers.

If the Response value equals the expected value, the authenticator MUST send Success (3). Otherwise it MUST send Failure (4) and SHOULD take action to terminate the link. Because a Success might be lost, the authenticator MUST allow repeated Responses in the Network-Layer Protocol phase and MUST return the same reply code for a Response with the current Challenge Identifier. Responses received in any other phase MUST be silently discarded.
sections.eli5: Each new question gets a new number, and the answer must carry the same number. Right answers get a yes, wrong ones get a no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says security is its primary topic. It notes that CHAP cannot protect against real-time active wiretapping, though unique, unpredictable challenges guard against a wide range of active attacks. The secret SHOULD NOT be the same in both directions, since that lets an attacker replay the peer's challenge and use the computed response.

There is no provision for retries of failed authentication, but LCP can renegotiate the authentication protocol at any time. A user name should be tied to exactly one authentication method, so that an attacker cannot push a user down to a weaker method such as PAP that would reveal a shared secret. Secrets should be stored and distributed so that as few parties as possible learn them.
sections.eli5: Do not use the same secret for both directions, and do not let a sneaky person trick you into using a weaker way of proving who you are.

messages.label: Response (Code 2)
messages.note: Hash of Identifier, secret and Challenge Value.

messages.label: Success (Code 3) or Failure (Code 4)
messages.note: Depends on whether the hash matches.

items.label: Challenge
items.desc: Sent by the authenticator to start the handshake.

items.label: Response
items.desc: The peer's hash of Identifier, secret and challenge.

items.label: Success
items.desc: The Response matched the expected value.

items.label: Failure
items.desc: The Response did not match; the link SHOULD be terminated.
